title: Young Kings: A Young Man's Guide to Dominion
author: Foster
summary: In this chapter excerpt from his book Young Kings, Foster uses his own experience with the 'high-place phenomenon' — the well-documented, non-suicidal urge roughly 40 to 50 percent of people feel to jump from a height — as a launching point for a broader argument about male self-governance. He recounts counseling a teenage boy who concluded he must be gay because intrusive gay thoughts flashed through his mind, and shows how he used his own experience with intrusive high-place urges to make the same point: an unbidden thought arising from within is not evidence of one's 'true self,' and acting on it is not required simply because it feels internally generated. Foster names this tension 'man versus himself' and argues that older stories understood the self as something to be mastered, resisted, or disciplined, while modern narratives — his explicit example is Frozen's 'Let It Go' — teach the opposite: that suppressed inner impulses are one's authentic self and should be expressed rather than governed. His theological argument turns on a close reading of two scriptures: Psalm 14:1's claim that a fool's heart can say there is no God, proving hearts can be simply wrong, contrasted with Proverbs 3's instruction to 'trust in the LORD with all your heart' — not to trust the heart itself, but to entrust it to God's authority. The chapter's practical conclusion for young men is that growing into godly manhood requires understanding, and actively governing, one's own heart rather than treating every internal impulse as authoritative.
points: Foster's parallel between his own non-suicidal 'high-place phenomenon' urge and a teenager's intrusive gay thoughts gives a memorable, concrete argument that an unbidden internal impulse is not proof of one's 'true self' or a claim that must be acted on.

His explicit critique of the Frozen 'Let It Go' narrative as emblematic of a modern reversal — from mastering the self to expressing whatever arises from within it — names a specific, widely recognized cultural script and positions the book's argument directly against it.

The scriptural contrast between Psalm 14:1 (a fool's heart can be simply wrong) and Proverbs 3 (trust the Lord *with* your heart, not the heart itself) gives the chapter's central claim — that the heart must be governed, not blindly followed — a specific theological grounding rather than a purely psychological one.
quotes: I was both surprised and relieved to learn that somewhere between 40 and 50% of people share this experience, sometimes called the call of the void or the high-place phenomenon.
In other words, even though death could occur if you followed through with that thought, the thought itself is not a secret, deep subconscious death wish.

Buddy, everyone has some weird gay thoughts pass through their mind from time to time. That doesn't mean you're gay. It means that you can't trust something just because it arises from within you, or appears to arise from within you.
there is something within me that I have been suppressing, and the resolution is to accept and express it. So instead of conquering yourself, it's about discovering yourself, your true self.
Psalm 14:1 says, "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'" So clearly, our hearts can be wrong. They are not always trustworthy.
It doesn't say to trust your heart. It says to trust the Lord with your heart. Your heart is not your highest authority. God is.
If you want to grow into a godly man, you must understand your heart, what it is, what it does, and why it must be governed rather than blindly followed.
